manuscript.working_title: Anthropogenic host redistribution expands butterfly resource geography across the specialization spectrum

scientific_state.resource_expansion: 206/239 butterflies expanded; aggregate butterfly×WGSRPD3 coverage +54.9% (14,553 added units)
scientific_state.host_contribution_concentration: 670 host species contribute; top 10=25.1%, top 50=57.0%, 38 species reach half; genus sensitivity 431 genera with 25 reaching half
scientific_state.diet_breadth_precision: rho=0.008; 49,999-bootstrap 95% CI -0.111 to 0.128; post-hoc ±0.10 TOST p=0.078, so exact equivalence is not claimed
scientific_state.phylogenetic_boundary: 124/239 exact Kawahara matches; fitted Pagel lambda=0.033, beta=-0.051 p=0.581; fixed Brownian beta=0.140 p=0.119 retained as boundary sensitivity
scientific_state.occurrence_validation: secondary climate-stratified panel; 66/115 outside-native units recovered; species-level region-matched null exceeded
scientific_state.network_prominence: exploratory explanatory hypothesis in Discussion/SI only
scientific_state.climate: secondary; filtering persists but host-breadth release prediction unsupported and imprecise
scientific_state.poaceae_sensitivity: 58 Poaceae users; excluding all leaves rho=0.026 (n=181), excluding 34 one-family Poaceae specialists leaves rho=0.013 (n=205)
scientific_state.conceptual_framework: taxonomic interaction breadth -> resource geography -> realized consumer geography; introduced host redistribution acts on resource geography while known host identities are held fixed
scientific_state.butterfly_family_generality: Expansion affected 83.5–90.2% of species in each of the five major butterfly families represented by at least 10 species (Nymphalidae, Hesperiidae, Pieridae, Lycaenidae, Papilionidae).
scientific_state.butterfly_first_implications: Discussion 4.3 links butterfly larval-resource geography to invasion ecology and conservation, while preserving the distinction between resource availability and demographic benefit.
scientific_state.crop_host_sensitivity: complete; FAO exact-binomial crop exclusion leaves +47.0% aggregate expansion, 203/238 evaluable butterflies expanded (85.3%), rho=0.052 and 38 host species accounting for half of added credit; conservative genus-expanded exclusion leaves +46.0%, 197/233 (84.5%), rho=0.057 and 37 hosts.
scientific_state.ruderal_non_crop_interpretation: Discussion now distinguishes the crop sensitivity from the broader residual signal: +47.0% to +46.0% aggregate expansion persists after crop-host exclusion. WCVP introduced records are wild non-native occurrences, making naturalized forage, pasture/turf, roadside/ruderal and escaped plants plausible contributors. No quantitative weed/ruderal attribution is claimed because non-crop hosts were not exhaustively classified by land use or introduction pathway.
scientific_state.conservation_implication: complete and bounded; vulnerability can be framed jointly by taxonomic specialization and host redistribution history; management implications are interaction-aware but do not recommend retaining invasive plants or infer host quality/fitness.
